strengths: Addresses a real and well-motivated problem: fragmentation of terminology (citation/attribution/quotation) in evidence-based text generation research, providing a much-needed unifying taxonomy across a large body of work (134 papers).

Methodologically grounded in an established systematic mapping study protocol (Petersen et al., 2008), with explicit search strings, multiple literature databases queried, and stated inclusion criteria, which supports reproducibility.

Broad and detailed coverage: taxonomy spans attribution approach, LLM integration strategy, five citation characteristics, and task types; evaluation section catalogs 300 metrics, 17 frameworks, 231 datasets, and 11 benchmarks with useful cross-tabulations (Figures 5-7, Tables 2-6).
Practical value for the community as a reference resource, with a public annotated dataset repository enabling verification and reuse.

Clear identification of concrete, actionable gaps (e.g., limited standardization of evaluation frameworks/benchmarks, underexplored parametric attribution, lack of citation explainability) that can guide future work.
Well-organized presentation with figures/tables that make the large amount of extracted information digestible.
weaknesses: The literature search is relatively narrow (a single boolean query on title/abstract with only three OR terms) and single-snapshot (February 2025), which risks missing relevant work using different terminology (e.g., 'grounding', 'faithfulness', 'provenance') despite querying nine databases; some databases (ICML, ScienceDirect) returned zero results, raising questions about search completeness or database coverage choices.

Reliability of the manual categorization is not quantified: only two annotators performed screening and labeling, and no inter-annotator agreement statistics are reported for the taxonomy assignment, which is important for a paper whose main contribution is a classification scheme.

The contribution is primarily descriptive/taxonomic; the Discussion section is relatively brief and largely restates known open problems (parametric attribution, standardization, explainability) rather than offering deeper synthesis, causal analysis, or a strong forward-looking research agenda beyond generic statements.

Some boundaries in the taxonomy (e.g., distinguishing in-generation, in-context, and post-retrieval attribution) appear somewhat fine-grained/subjective and could be contested by other researchers, and this is not stress-tested via inter-annotator or ablation checks.

There appear to be minor internal inconsistencies in reported counts across sections (e.g., parametric attribution counts differ between the Figure 5 breakdown and the discussion text), which slightly undermines confidence in the numerical precision of the analysis.

Given the rapid pace of LLM research and a February 2025 cutoff, portions of the taxonomy and trend analysis risk becoming quickly dated, somewhat limiting the survey's longevity relative to the stated ambition of being a definitive reference.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important gap: the paper is (to the authors' knowledge) the first comprehensive, systematic survey unifying the fragmented terminology of citation-, attribution-, and quotation-based evidence generation with LLMs.

Rigorous methodology grounded in an established systematic mapping study protocol (Petersen et al. 2008), with explicit search strings, multiple literature databases, and stated inclusion/exclusion criteria, improving transparency and reproducibility.

Impressive scale and breadth of the analysis: 134 papers, 300 evaluation metrics, 17 frameworks, 231 datasets, and 11 benchmarks are systematically categorized, providing a genuinely useful reference resource for the community.

The taxonomy meaningfully extends prior categorizations (e.g., splitting parametric attribution into three subtypes, adding in-generation and in-context non-parametric categories) rather than simply restating existing frameworks.

The evaluation-metrics section (Section 6) is particularly valuable, mapping methods to dimensions and identifying which metric clusters are complementary, which is a common pain point in this literature.
Public release of the annotated dataset supports reproducibility and follow-up work.

The discussion section identifies concrete, well-motivated future directions (parametric attribution, evaluation standardization, explainable citations) grounded in the quantitative findings rather than generic statements.
weaknesses: The literature search string is narrow (title/abstract match on a fixed set of terms) and the near-zero yield from several major databases (ICML, ScienceDirect) raises concern about coverage gaps rather than genuine absence of relevant work in those venues.

Screening and categorization were performed by only two authors with disagreements resolved jointly; no inter-annotator agreement statistic is reported, which limits confidence in the reliability/reproducibility of the fine-grained taxonomy labels (especially for subjective dimensions like citation style or contribution type).

The critical synthesis in Section 7 is relatively brief given the scale of data collected; deeper cross-cutting analysis (e.g., correlations between task type and metric reliability, or systematic critique of which metrics are actually valid proxies for human judgment) is missing.

The taxonomy, while extended, is explicitly built by incrementally modifying existing frameworks (Huang and Chang 2024; Li et al. 2023) rather than being a fundamentally new conceptual contribution, somewhat limiting novelty.

Given only a single cutoff (February 2025) and the field's stated fast growth (106 papers in 2024 alone), the survey risks becoming quickly dated, and there is limited discussion of how the resource will be maintained or updated.

Some figures (e.g., the four-panel taxonomy figure and the evaluation metrics figure) are dense and could be difficult to parse without extended study, which may hinder accessibility for readers seeking quick reference.

strengths: Rigorous and transparent systematic review methodology: PRISMA-style flow, explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria, inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha) reported for both screening and taxonomy annotation, and a sensitivity analysis testing an expanded search string to gauge coverage risk.

Large, carefully curated corpus (134 papers, 300 metrics, 231 datasets, 19 frameworks, 11 benchmarks) that fills a genuine gap, since prior surveys/position papers (Huang and Chang 2024; Li et al. 2023a) are outdated (pre-2024) and narrower in scope.

The proposed multidimensional, facetted taxonomy (attribution approach x citation characteristics x task) is a reasonable and practically useful organizing scheme that extends existing parametric/non-parametric distinctions with new subcategories (e.g., in-generation, in-context attribution) grounded in the annotated corpus.

Extensive, well-organized evaluation-metric analysis (Section 5 and Appendix E) that maps metrics to seven evaluation dimensions and six methods, along with practical guidelines (Table 1) for which dimensions to report given task/evidence availability — a genuinely useful resource for the community.
Public release of the annotated dataset, promoting reproducibility and future reuse of the survey's categorization scheme.

Reasonable identification of concrete, actionable future directions (parametric/hybrid attribution, standardized evaluation, explainable citations, multimodal evidence) grounded in the quantitative trends observed.
weaknesses: The core contribution is largely descriptive/cataloguing (frequency counts, taxonomy labels, temporal trend plots) rather than deeper critical synthesis; e.g., there is limited analysis of comparative performance, correlations between metrics, or methodological quality/rigor of the surveyed approaches beyond category counts.

The single primary search string, while validated by a sensitivity check, still restricts venue coverage to two databases for the sensitivity test and nine databases overall; some important adjacent literatures (e.g., grounding, hallucination detection with strong overlap) may be under-sampled, and the claimed genericity of the taxonomy is not stress-tested against these alternate literatures.

Contribution novelty relative to existing categorizations (Huang and Chang 2024; Li et al. 2023a) is incremental in places — the paper explicitly builds on and extends prior parametric/non-parametric and post-retrieval/post-generation distinctions rather than introducing a fundamentally new conceptual framework.

Given the extremely fast-moving nature of this field (as the paper itself notes, with a 3.4x year-over-year growth and search conducted in Feb 2025), the survey's currency will degrade quickly, and by publication many of the 'open challenges' identified (e.g., in-generation attribution, multimodal citation) may already be addressed by newer work not captured.

The evaluation-dimension guidelines (Table 1) and taxonomy, while useful, are somewhat prescriptive without strong empirical validation (e.g., no demonstration that following these guidelines improves comparability across a concrete case study of several systems).

Inter-annotator agreement was computed only on subsets (30–50 papers) with just two annotators who are also authors, which may inflate agreement scores relative to independent external annotators; some Krippendorff's alpha values (e.g., 0.73, 0.77, 0.79) are only moderate.
